title: Separable verbs
theoryMd:
German builds a huge amount of its vocabulary by gluing a short prefix onto a verb. *Stehen* means to stand; *aufstehen* means to get up; *verstehen* means to understand; *bestehen* means to pass (an exam). One stem, three unrelated meanings.

Some of these prefixes **detach** from the verb when you use it in a sentence, and some never do. Which group a prefix belongs to is fixed, and knowing the two lists is most of the battle.

## Separable prefixes

These are mostly prepositions and adverbs you already know as independent words. They are **stressed** in speech: ***AUF**stehen*, ***AN**rufen*.

*ab-, an-, auf-, aus-, bei-, ein-, mit-, nach-, vor-, zu-, zurück-, weg-, hin-, her-, los-, fest-, statt-, teil-, zusammen-*

In a main clause the prefix leaves the verb and goes to the **very end** of the sentence:

- *Ich **rufe** dich morgen **an**.* (anrufen — to call)
- *Sie **steht** jeden Tag um sechs Uhr **auf**.* (aufstehen — to get up)
- *Wir **kaufen** am Samstag **ein**.* (einkaufen — to shop)

The further apart they land, the more German the sentence feels: *Ich **rufe** dich morgen nach der Arbeit von zu Hause aus **an**.*

## Inseparable prefixes

These never detach. They are **unstressed**, and none of them exists as a standalone word:

*be-, emp-, ent-, er-, ge-, miss-, ver-, zer-*

- *Ich **verstehe** dich nicht.*
- *Sie **bezahlt** die Rechnung.*
- *Er **erklärt** die Aufgabe.*

A memory hook: **"Ge-be-er-ver-zer-ent-emp-miss"** — say it a few times and it sticks. Everything else separates.

> The stress test is reliable and instant: if you hear the stress on the prefix, it separates. *Ich **ÜBER**setze den Text* (I ferry the text across) vs *Ich über**SETZ**e den Text* (I translate it). A handful of prefixes — *über-, unter-, um-, durch-, wieder-* — can go either way, and the meaning changes with the stress. Literal meaning → separable; figurative meaning → inseparable.

## Where the prefix goes

The prefix's position depends entirely on the clause type. Four cases cover everything.

**1. Main clause — prefix at the end**

> *Ich **stehe** um sieben Uhr **auf**.*

**2. Subordinate clause — the verb rejoins its prefix at the end**

> *…, weil ich um sieben Uhr **aufstehe**.*

Because the conjugated verb goes to the end anyway, it meets the prefix there and the word becomes whole again.

**3. With a modal verb — infinitive stays whole at the end**

> *Ich **muss** um sieben Uhr **aufstehen**.*

**4. Perfekt — the *ge-* goes in the middle**

This is the detail people forget. The participle marker *ge-* is inserted **between** the prefix and the stem:

> *Ich **bin** um sieben Uhr **aufgestanden**.*
> *Ich **habe** dich gestern **angerufen**.*

Inseparable verbs, by contrast, take **no *ge-* at all**: *verstanden*, *bezahlt*, *erklärt* — never *geverstanden*.

The same applies to *zu* in infinitive clauses, which also slots into the middle:

> *Ich versuche, früh **aufzustehen**.* (not *zu aufstehen*)
> But: *Ich versuche, dich **zu verstehen**.*

## Why the meaning shifts so much

Prefixes are not decoration; they change meaning in ways you cannot always predict:

| Verb | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **kommen** | to come |
| **an**kommen | to arrive |
| **be**kommen | to receive (a false friend — *not* "to become") |
| **mit**kommen | to come along |
| **um**kommen | to die, to perish |

Some patterns do recur and are worth noticing:

- **auf-** often means opening or upward motion: *aufmachen* (open), *aufstehen* (stand up), *aufwachen* (wake up)
- **zu-** often means closing: *zumachen* (close), *zubinden* (tie shut)
- **weg-** and **ab-** suggest going away: *weggehen*, *abfahren*
- **ver-** frequently marks something going wrong or being used up: *sich verlaufen* (get lost), *verschlafen* (oversleep), *verbrauchen* (use up)
- **zer-** always means breaking apart: *zerbrechen*, *zerreißen*, *zerstören*

When you save a new prefixed verb, it is worth checking whether you already know the base verb. Learning *stehen → aufstehen → verstehen → bestehen* as a family is far more efficient than meeting each as an unrelated word.

payload.explanation: an- is separable, so in a main clause the prefix goes to the very end.

payload.prompt: Sie steht jeden Tag um sechs Uhr ___ . (aufstehen)
payload.explanation: auf- separates and lands at the end of the main clause.
ver- is one of the inseparable prefixes (ge-, be-, er-, ver-, zer-, ent-, emp-, miss-). The others all separate.

payload.prompt: Perfekt of 'anrufen': Ich habe dich gestern ___ .
payload.explanation: In a separable verb the ge- goes between prefix and stem: an + ge + rufen = angerufen.

payload.prompt: Perfekt of 'verstehen': Ich habe dich nicht ___ .
payload.explanation: Inseparable verbs take no ge- at all: verstanden, bezahlt, erklärt.

payload.prompt: Subordinate clause: …, weil ich um sieben Uhr ___ . (aufstehen)
payload.explanation: In a subordinate clause the conjugated verb goes to the end and rejoins its prefix: aufstehe.

payload.prompt: With a modal: Ich muss um sieben Uhr ___ . (aufstehen)
payload.explanation: After a modal the verb stays as a whole infinitive at the end — no separation.
In a zu-infinitive the zu slots between prefix and stem: auf-zu-stehen.
A classic false friend: bekommen = to receive. 'to become' is werden.
The separable prefix goes to the very end, after the time expression.

payload.prompt: You hear the stress on the prefix: ÜBERsetzen. What does it mean?
payload.explanation: Stress on the prefix means separable and literal. Unstressed über-SETZ-en is inseparable and means 'to translate'.
zer- always signals destruction: zerbrechen, zerreißen, zerstören.
